panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast CT of the head/neck (caption says 'sagittal', but the displayed plane is coronal with R/L markers) from a real patient, with red arrows marking both parotid regions. Bilateral parotid gland enlargement is a classic, specific manifestation of Sjögren's syndrome and matches the vocabulary finding sjogren_syndrome_parotid_gland_enlargement; the disease-focused article title (Primary Sjögren's Syndrome) plus the captioned manifestation support attribution to sjogren_syndrome, subtype primary. No age or ethnicity is stated; not a skin panel. Confidence slightly tempered because the article also involves IgG4-RD, which can enlarge parotids, but the configured target and prior triage attribute this panel to primary Sjögren's. panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT panel (red arrows and asterisk annotation) from a case report of pediatric SLE with Sjögren's overlap. The image visibly demonstrates bilateral parotid enlargement with heterogeneous hypodense parenchyma—the CT correlate of the recognized Sjögren's sialadenitis pattern—together with intraparenchymal microcalcifications, plus an incidental right maxillary sinus inflammatory density. Attribution to Sjögren's rests on the disease-focused article title combined with the specific captioned glandular manifestation ('inflammatory glandular involvement'); no other disease is named for this panel, quality is diagnostic, and the source is open-access. Mild uncertainty remains because the pneumococcal-sepsis context could also explain parotid inflammation, and the caption does not explicitly say 'Sjögren's sialadenitis'; age is not stated in the caption or in-text, so age_group is unknown despite the pediatric title. [raw subtype: secondary (overlap with systemic lupus erythematosus)]

Final pathology reported “abscess, features consistent with Sjögren syndrome, and two benign intraparotid lymph nodes.” Her operative site has healed well, and there has been no further recurrence of symptoms.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (Top left, Top right, Bottom left, Bottom right). Top left: H&E low/high-power view of labial minor salivary gland with lymphoid aggregates described as suggestive of Sjogren's syndrome, matching focal lymphocytic sialadenitis. Top right: High-power H&E of same diagnostic labial biopsy suggestive of Sjogren's; caption notes mucinous acini with foamy macrophages, background chronic lymphocytic infiltrate supports periductal lymphocytic sialadenitis. Bottom left: Intermediate magnification H&E of same Sjogren-suggestive labial biopsy showing mucinous acini with atrophied glands in fibrotic stroma with lymphoid infiltrate visible, part of focal lymphocytic sialadenitis spectrum. Bottom right: Intermediate magnification H&E of same Sjogren-suggestive labial biopsy showing mucinous acini with atrophied glands in fibrotic stroma with lymphoid infiltrate visible.

panels.figure_caption: Sections from the minor salivary gland show mucinous acini with abundant foamy macrophages (top right), lymphoid aggregates in a background of interstitial fibrosis (top left), and mucinous acini with a few atrophied glands (bottom right and left images), suggestive of Sjögren's syndrome Histopathological examination of minor labial salivary gland tissue (Hematoxylin & Eosin stain). (Top right) Low-power view (4x objective). (Top left) High-power view (40x objective). (Below right and left) Intermediate magnification (10x-20x objective). Scale bars: top right=200 µm, top left=20 µm, below right and left=50 µm.
in_text_mentions: A labial mucosa biopsy was also performed, which showed minor salivary glands surrounded by moderate chronic lymphocytic infiltrate and lymphoid aggregates. Fibrosis was also noticed along with atrophy of the glands (Figure 5). The histopathological diagnostic criteria for Sjögren syndrome rely on the presence of focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (FLS) with a focus score ≥1 per 4 mm² of glandular tissue [7].

in_text_mentions: The lung CT in October 2024 revealed multiple cystic lucencies in both lungs. In combination with the medical history of pSS, this was initially suggestive of lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (Figure 4). Follow-up CT revealed that emphysema and diffuse multiple cystic spaces in both lungs, so lymphoid interstitial lung disease was considered (Figure 5).
